🚗 Task 3 · Car Price Prediction with Machine Learning¶

Objective: Build a regression model that predicts the selling price of a used car from features such as brand, age, kilometres driven, fuel type and transmission.

Tech stack: Python · pandas · scikit-learn · matplotlib · seaborn · Jupyter Notebook

Dataset: Vehicle dataset from CarDekho (Kaggle) — file car data.csv, 301 used-vehicle listings.

Download car data.csv from Kaggle and place it in the data/ folder next to this notebook.

Column Meaning
Car_Name Model name (e.g. swift, city)
Year Year of manufacture
Selling_Price Target — price the owner is selling at (₹ lakh)
Present_Price Current ex-showroom price of the same model, new (₹ lakh)
Kms_Driven Kilometres driven (mileage)
Fuel_Type Petrol / Diesel / CNG
Seller_Type Dealer / Individual
Transmission Manual / Automatic
Owner Number of previous owners

Notebook outline¶

  1. Setup & data loading
  2. Data cleaning — nulls, duplicates, inconsistent categories
  3. Feature engineering — car age, brand, cars vs two-wheelers
  4. EDA — price distribution, price vs fuel type, price vs age
  5. Encoding categorical variables (One-Hot)
  6. Correlation heatmap
  7. Train / test split
  8. Model training — Linear Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting
  9. Evaluation — MAE, RMSE, R² (+ cross-validation)
  10. Feature importance of the best model
  11. Sample prediction & conclusion

2. Data Cleaning¶

2.1 Null values¶

In [5]:
print("Missing values per column:")
print(df_raw.isnull().sum())

df = df_raw.copy()
# Generic, safe handling (does nothing here, but makes the pipeline robust to a dataset with gaps):
# numeric -> fill with median, categorical -> fill with mode
for col in df.columns:
    if df[col].isnull().any():
        if df[col].dtype == "object":
            df[col] = df[col].fillna(df[col].mode()[0])
        else:
            df[col] = df[col].fillna(df[col].median())
print("\nMissing values after handling:", df.isnull().sum().sum())

# Standardise text columns:
#  - strip leading/trailing spaces, collapse repeated spaces
#  - categorical columns -> one canonical spelling ('petrol' / 'PETROL ' -> 'Petrol', 'cng' -> 'CNG')
#  - car names -> lower case so 'Activa 4g' and 'activa 4G' would match
df["Car_Name"] = (df["Car_Name"].str.strip()
                                .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
                                .str.lower())

CANONICAL = {"petrol": "Petrol", "diesel": "Diesel", "cng": "CNG", "lpg": "LPG", "electric": "Electric",
             "dealer": "Dealer", "individual": "Individual", "trustmark dealer": "Trustmark Dealer",
             "manual": "Manual", "automatic": "Automatic"}

for col in ["Fuel_Type", "Seller_Type", "Transmission"]:
    lowered = df[col].str.strip().str.lower()
    df[col] = lowered.map(CANONICAL).fillna(lowered.str.title())   # unknown values -> Title Case
    print(col, "->", df[col].unique())

3. Feature Engineering¶

3.1 Brand extraction and separating two-wheelers¶

In this dataset, two-wheelers (bikes/scooters) are listed with the brand in the name ("Royal Enfield Classic 350", "Bajaj Pulsar 150"), while cars are listed by model only ("swift", "city", "fortuner"). So:

  • For two-wheelers → brand = first word(s) of the name.
  • For cars → brand is looked up from the model name with a small mapping (e.g. swift → Maruti, city → Honda).

Because the task is car price prediction and a ₹0.5-lakh scooter behaves very differently from a ₹10-lakh SUV, the two-wheelers are identified and removed before modelling.

In [9]:
# Brands of the two-wheelers present in the data ('activa' is Honda's scooter)
BIKE_BRANDS = ["royal enfield", "hero honda", "bajaj", "hero", "honda", "yamaha", "tvs",
               "ktm", "suzuki", "hyosung", "mahindra", "um", "activa"]

# Car model -> brand mapping for every car model in the dataset
CAR_BRANDS = {
    "Maruti":  ["800", "alto 800", "alto k10", "baleno", "ciaz", "dzire", "ertiga", "ignis",
                "omni", "ritz", "s cross", "swift", "sx4", "vitara brezza", "wagon r"],
    "Hyundai": ["creta", "elantra", "eon", "grand i10", "i10", "i20", "verna", "xcent"],
    "Honda":   ["amaze", "brio", "city", "jazz"],
    "Toyota":  ["camry", "corolla", "corolla altis", "etios cross", "etios g", "etios gd",
                "etios liva", "fortuner", "innova", "land cruiser"],
}
MODEL_TO_BRAND = {model: brand for brand, models in CAR_BRANDS.items() for model in models}

def classify(name: str):
    """Return (vehicle_type, brand) for a cleaned, lower-case vehicle name."""
    if name in MODEL_TO_BRAND:
        return "Car", MODEL_TO_BRAND[name]
    for b in BIKE_BRANDS:
        if name.startswith(b):
            return "Two-Wheeler", ("Honda" if b == "activa" else b.title())
    return "Unknown", "Other"

df[["Vehicle_Type", "Brand"]] = df["Car_Name"].apply(lambda n: pd.Series(classify(n)))
df["Vehicle_Type"].value_counts()

3.2 Car age from the Year column¶

Car_Age = REFERENCE_YEAR − Year. The listings were collected around 2019 (newest car is a 2018 model), so 2019 is used as the reference year — this gives the car's age at the time it was listed, which is what drove its price. (Using today's year would just add the same constant to every car and wouldn't change the models.)

In [12]:
REFERENCE_YEAR = 2019
cars["Car_Age"] = REFERENCE_YEAR - cars["Year"]

Prices are strongly right-skewed — most cars sell for ₹3–8 lakh, with a long tail of premium cars (Fortuner, Land Cruiser) up to ₹35 lakh. A log transform makes the distribution much more symmetric; this is used for Linear Regression later.

EDA observations

  • Age ↓ price: older cars sell for less — a clear negative trend (depreciation).
  • Present price is the strongest driver: selling price rises almost linearly with the new-car price, always sitting below the Selling = Present line.
  • Diesel cars have a higher median price than petrol (diesels in this data are mostly larger SUVs/sedans like Fortuner, Innova). CNG has only 2 cars — too few to draw conclusions.
  • Automatic cars and Toyota cars command higher prices.

5. Encoding Categorical Variables¶

One-Hot Encoding (pd.get_dummies) is used because Fuel_Type, Seller_Type, Transmission and Brand are nominal — there is no natural order (Diesel isn't "greater than" Petrol). Label encoding would invent a fake order that would mislead Linear Regression. drop_first=True drops one level per feature to avoid the dummy variable trap (perfect multicollinearity).

Columns dropped: Car_Name (too many unique values for 200 rows — its information is captured by Brand and Present_Price) and Year (replaced by Car_Age).

In [16]:
model_df = cars.drop(columns=["Car_Name", "Year"])
model_df = pd.get_dummies(model_df, columns=["Fuel_Type", "Seller_Type", "Transmission", "Brand"],
                          drop_first=True, dtype=int)
print("Encoded shape:", model_df.shape)
model_df.head()

Heatmap takeaways

  • Present_Price has the highest positive correlation with Selling_Price — a new-car price is the starting point for a used-car price.
  • Fuel_Type_Petrol is negative while diesel (the dropped baseline) is positive, matching the box plot.
  • Car_Age is negatively correlated (depreciation), and Transmission_Manual is negative (automatics cost more).
  • Kms_Driven correlates with age (older cars have been driven more) — a mild multicollinearity worth noting for Linear Regression.

7. Train / Test Split (80 / 20)¶

In [18]:
X = model_df.drop(columns="Selling_Price")
y = model_df["Selling_Price"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
print("Train:", X_train.shape, "| Test:", X_test.shape)

Train: (158, 11) | Test: (40, 11)

8. Model Training¶

Model Idea
Linear Regression (log-log) Fits a weighted sum. Prices are skewed and depreciation is multiplicative (a car loses a % of its value per year, not a fixed ₹ amount), so the model is trained on log(price) with log(Present_Price) and log(Kms_Driven) as inputs. Predictions are converted back to ₹ lakh with expm1.
Random Forest Regressor Averages many decision trees trained on random subsets → captures non-linear effects, robust to outliers.
Gradient Boosting Regressor Builds trees one after another, each correcting the previous one's errors → usually the most accurate on tabular data.

Tree models don't need feature scaling or a log target.

Why log-log? A plain Linear Regression on raw prices reaches only R² ≈ 0.82 in cross-validation, and using a log target alone breaks down on the ₹92.6-lakh Land Cruiser (a huge raw input pushed through exp). Taking logs on both sides turns "price falls by a % each year" into a straight line — exactly what Linear Regression can fit.

In [19]:
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor, ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

# Linear Regression (log-log):
#   inputs : log1p() applied to the two skewed money/distance columns, other columns passed through
#   target : log1p(price) during training, converted back with expm1() at prediction time
log_features = ColumnTransformer([("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p), ["Present_Price", "Kms_Driven"])],
                                 remainder="passthrough")
log_log_lr = TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=make_pipeline(log_features, LinearRegression()),
                                        func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1)

models = {
    "Linear Regression": log_log_lr,
    "Random Forest": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=400, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Gradient Boosting": GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05,
                                                   max_depth=3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}

predictions = {}
for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    predictions[name] = model.predict(X_test)
    print(f"✔ Trained: {name}")

✔ Trained: Linear Regression

✔ Trained: Random Forest

✔ Trained: Gradient Boosting

9. Model Evaluation — MAE, RMSE, R²¶

Metric Meaning Better
MAE (Mean Absolute Error) Average size of the error, in ₹ lakh Lower
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) Like MAE but penalises big errors more heavily Lower
R² (Coefficient of determination) Share of price variation the model explains (1.0 = perfect) Higher
In [20]:
def evaluate(y_true, y_pred):
    return {"MAE (₹ lakh)": mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred),
            "RMSE (₹ lakh)": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)),
            "R²": r2_score(y_true, y_pred)}

results = pd.DataFrame({name: evaluate(y_test, p) for name, p in predictions.items()}).T
results.round(4)
Out[20]:
MAE (₹ lakh) RMSE (₹ lakh) R²
Linear Regression 1.0240 1.8074 0.9032
Random Forest 1.0621 2.5279 0.8106
Gradient Boosting 1.1509 2.8421 0.7606

9.1 Cross-validation¶

With only ~40 cars in the test set, one split can be lucky or unlucky. 5-fold cross-validation on all the data gives a more reliable comparison.

In [21]:
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
for name, model in models.items():
    r2_cv  = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="r2")
    mae_cv = -cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
    results.loc[name, "CV R² (mean)"]  = r2_cv.mean()
    results.loc[name, "CV R² (std)"]   = r2_cv.std()
    results.loc[name, "CV MAE (mean)"] = mae_cv.mean()

results = results.sort_values("CV R² (mean)", ascending=False)
results.round(4)

10. Best Model & Feature Importance¶

In [24]:
best_name = results["CV R² (mean)"].idxmax()
best_model = models[best_name]
print(f"🏆 Best model: {best_name}")
print(results.loc[best_name].round(4).to_string())

🏆 Best model: Linear Regression
MAE (₹ lakh)     1.0240
RMSE (₹ lakh)    1.8074
R²               0.9032
CV R² (mean)     0.9367
CV R² (std)      0.0206
CV MAE (mean)    0.8247

Linear Regression has no built-in feature_importances_, so permutation importance is used: shuffle one feature at a time on the test set and measure how much R² drops. A big drop = the model relies heavily on that feature. This works for any model, so the same method is applied to the best tree model for comparison.

In [25]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

perm = permutation_importance(best_model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=30,
                              random_state=RANDOM_STATE, scoring="r2")
importance = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=True)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))
colors = ["#D1495B" if v == importance.max() else "#4C9F70" for v in importance]
importance.plot(kind="barh", color=colors)
plt.title(f"Feature Importance — {best_name}")
plt.xlabel("Mean drop in R² when the feature is shuffled")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(4)

🏆 Best model: Linear Regression (log-log)

Model Test MAE Test RMSE Test R² 5-fold CV R² CV MAE
Linear Regression (log-log) 1.02 1.81 0.903 0.937 ± 0.021 0.82
Gradient Boosting 1.15 2.84 0.761 0.889 ± 0.062 0.87
Random Forest 1.06 2.53 0.811 0.863 ± 0.061 0.93

Justification

  1. Best on every metric — lowest MAE and RMSE, highest R² on the test set and the highest cross-validated R² (0.937).
  2. Most stable — its CV standard deviation (0.021) is one-third of the tree models' (~0.06), so its accuracy doesn't depend on a lucky split.
  3. It matches how depreciation actually works. Used-car prices fall by a percentage per year. In log space that becomes a straight line, which Linear Regression fits perfectly with only ~160 training cars, while trees need far more data to learn the same smooth curve.
  4. It can extrapolate; trees can't. The test set contains a Land Cruiser (new price ₹92.6 lakh, sold at ₹35 lakh), far pricier than any car the models trained on. Trees can never predict above the prices they saw (RF ≈ ₹20 lakh, GB ≈ ₹19 lakh), while the log-log model predicted ≈ ₹26 lakh — still under, but much closer. This one car explains most of the gap between the trees' test R² and their CV R².
  5. Interpretable — every coefficient has a business meaning (table above): +1% new-car price → +0.75% selling price, each extra year of age → about −7.7%, each previous owner → about −16%, and diesel → about +29% vs the CNG baseline.

Feature importance: Present_Price dominates by far, followed by Fuel type (Diesel) and Car age. Gradient Boosting's own importance ranking agrees: Present_Price first, Car_Age second. Kms_Driven, Owner, Seller type and Brand add little once the new-car price is known (brand is largely already "priced in" through Present_Price).

Exam one-liner: Small dataset + multiplicative depreciation → log-log Linear Regression beat Random Forest & Gradient Boosting; trees can't extrapolate beyond the target range they were trained on.

11. Sample Prediction¶

In [28]:
def predict_price(present_price, kms_driven, owner, car_age, fuel, seller, transmission, brand):
    """Build one row with the same encoded columns as training data and predict its price."""
    row = pd.DataFrame(0, index=[0], columns=X.columns)
    row["Present_Price"], row["Kms_Driven"], row["Owner"], row["Car_Age"] = present_price, kms_driven, owner, car_age
    for col in [f"Fuel_Type_{fuel}", f"Seller_Type_{seller}", f"Transmission_{transmission}", f"Brand_{brand}"]:
        if col in row.columns:          # baseline categories (dropped by drop_first) stay all-zero
            row[col] = 1
    return best_model.predict(row)[0]

examples = pd.DataFrame([
    dict(present_price=7.0,  kms_driven=35000, owner=0, car_age=4, fuel="Petrol", seller="Dealer",     transmission="Manual",    brand="Maruti"),
    dict(present_price=10.5, kms_driven=60000, owner=0, car_age=6, fuel="Diesel", seller="Dealer",     transmission="Manual",    brand="Hyundai"),
    dict(present_price=30.0, kms_driven=45000, owner=0, car_age=3, fuel="Diesel", seller="Dealer",     transmission="Automatic", brand="Toyota"),
    dict(present_price=5.0,  kms_driven=80000, owner=1, car_age=9, fuel="Petrol", seller="Individual", transmission="Manual",    brand="Honda"),
])
examples["Predicted Selling Price (₹ lakh)"] = [round(predict_price(**r), 2) for r in examples.to_dict("records")]
examples

12. Conclusion¶

  • Data cleaning: no nulls; 2 duplicate rows removed; car names and categorical text standardised (spaces, case).
  • Feature engineering: Car_Age derived from Year; Brand extracted from the vehicle name (with a model→brand map for cars); two-wheelers identified and excluded so the model focuses on cars.
  • EDA: prices are right-skewed; price falls with age, rises with present (new) price; diesel and automatic cars sell higher.
  • Models: Linear Regression (on log price), Random Forest and Gradient Boosting were compared using MAE, RMSE, R² and 5-fold cross-validation.
  • Best model: Linear Regression (log-log) — test R² 0.903, MAE ₹1.02 lakh, 5-fold CV R² 0.937. On this small dataset, modelling depreciation as a percentage (log scale) beat the tree ensembles, which also can't extrapolate to very expensive cars. Present price, fuel type and car age are the dominant features.

Possible extensions: hyperparameter tuning (GridSearchCV), the larger CarDekho v3/v4 datasets (with engine, mileage and power), and deploying the model with Streamlit as a price-estimator app.
